hazards.lead-the-answer: You asked a question that suggested its own answer. A leading question puts your idea into their memory and makes the recording less trustworthy; open questions like how, what and tell me about let them say what they actually remember.
hazards.memory-is-a-fact: You wrote the memory down as a proved fact. Memories are precious evidence of how things felt and what mattered, but they change over time; a historian checks them against other sources, just as they would a document.
hazards.record-without-asking: You started recording before asking permission. An oral history belongs to the person telling it; they decide whether they are recorded, what is kept and who may hear it. Consent comes first, every time, and it can be withdrawn.
hazards.share-without-permission: You wanted to post a clip online without asking. The interviewee agreed to a class archive, not the internet; sharing beyond what they agreed breaks their trust and their consent. Ask first, and respect the answer.

interrupts.alert: The interviewee's voice catches while describing a hard time at work, and they look upset.
interrupts.cue: Pause the recording and gently offer to stop or take a break.
interrupts.missNote: You pressed on with the next question, and the interviewee ended the session upset.
interrupts.why: An interviewee's wellbeing matters more than the recording. Pausing and offering a break or an end gives them control, and it is what every oral history guide asks interviewers to do.
interrupts.wrongNote: That carries on regardless. Pause and offer to stop. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: The oral history volunteer asks what the interviewee agreed to and who may hear the recording.
interrupts.cue: Say what the consent form covers and who may hear it.
interrupts.missNote: You were not sure, and the volunteer had to check the form before anything could be kept.
interrupts.why: The volunteer is checking you know the limits of consent. Saying exactly what was agreed shows the recording will be used only as the interviewee wished.
interrupts.wrongNote: That does not say what was agreed. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.koh-archive-log: The archive notes are written once the interview is over — nothing to record yet.
lateNotes.koh-checkin: The check-in comes at the very end of the session.

name: Oral History Interview Skills

steps.cue: Mark the three things you need ready before the interview begins.

decoyNotes.koh-union-banner: A striking thing to ask about later, but not something you need ready to start.

itemNames.koh-question-list: a short list of open questions

itemNotes.koh-consent-form: It records what the interviewee agrees to.
itemNotes.koh-question-list: Open questions let them tell it their way.
itemNotes.koh-recorder: Check it works before, not during.

steps.prompt: Mark the three things you need ready before the interview begins.
steps.title: Find what you need before the interview
steps.why: A good interview is prepared. A consent form sets out what will be recorded and who may hear it, a short list of open questions keeps the conversation focused without controlling it, and a working recorder means the words are kept. With those three ready, you can give your full attention to listening.

steps.cue: Consent, an easy opening, open questions with follow-ups, then thank and check.

itemNames.koh-ord-open: 3 · ask open questions and follow up
itemNames.koh-ord-opening: 2 · start with an easy opening question
itemNames.koh-ord-thank: 4 · thank them and check what may be shared

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. Consent comes before anything is recorded.
steps.prompt: Consent, an easy opening, open questions with follow-ups, then thank and check.
steps.title: Put the interview in order
steps.why: Consent first makes the interview possible. An easy opening, such as asking where they grew up, helps the interviewee relax. Open questions and follow-ups draw out detail, and a thank-you with a check of what they are happy to share closes it respectfully.

steps.cue: Explain what the recording is for and ask the interviewee to agree before you press record.
steps.prompt: Explain what the recording is for and ask the interviewee to agree before you press record.
steps.title: Ask for consent before recording
steps.why: Consent is the foundation of oral history. Explaining clearly what the recording is for, who will hear it and that they can stop at any time lets the interviewee make a real choice, and it is how every responsible archive works.

steps.cue: Turn the recording level so their voice is clear without distorting.
steps.prompt: Turn the recording level so their voice is clear without distorting.
steps.title: Turn the recorder's level to their voice
steps.why: A recording that is too quiet loses words, and one that is too loud distorts them. Setting the level to the interviewee's voice before the main questions means their words will be heard clearly by everyone who listens later.

steps.cue: Commit when the level meter sits in the band as they speak.

gauge.label: VOICE
gauge.missNote: Outside the band. Adjust the level before the main questions.

steps.prompt: Commit when the level meter sits in the band as they speak.
steps.title: Check the voice level is in the band
steps.why: A level meter shows whether the voice is being recorded well. Checking it while they speak, not only in silence, catches a quiet speaker or a noisy room before the whole interview is spoiled.

steps.cue: Stay quiet and hold the pause while the interviewee gathers their thoughts.
steps.holdBreakNote: You filled the silence too soon. Let them think, and hold the pause again.
steps.prompt: Stay quiet and hold the pause while the interviewee gathers their thoughts.
steps.title: Hold the pause while they think
steps.why: The best part of an answer often comes after a pause. Staying quiet and letting the silence sit gives the interviewee time to remember, instead of jumping in with another question that cuts off what they were about to say.

steps.cue: Drag the open follow-up card into the question slot.

drag.missNote: Not in the slot yet. Put the open follow-up in the next question.

steps.prompt: Drag the open follow-up card into the question slot.
steps.title: Choose an open follow-up question
steps.why: A follow-up like tell me more about that invites detail in the interviewee's own words. Choosing it over a yes or no question keeps the story theirs, and it is the single most useful habit of a good interviewer.

steps.cue: Look at the draft interview plan and mark each problem.

decoyNotes.koh-ip-thanks: Thanking the interviewee is good practice. Keep it.

itemNames.koh-ip-leading: a question that suggests its answer
itemNames.koh-ip-share: a plan to post clips online

steps.prompt: Look at the draft interview plan and mark each problem.
steps.title: Spot the problems in a classmate's interview plan
steps.why: Interview plans go wrong in familiar ways: no consent step, leading questions and a plan to share recordings more widely than agreed. Spotting them helps you plan an interview that is both good history and respectful of the person.

steps.cue: Say what a memory can tell a historian, and what it needs checking against.
steps.prompt: Say what a memory can tell a historian, and what it needs checking against.
steps.title: Say how a memory is a source
steps.why: A memory tells you how something felt and what mattered to the person who lived it, which documents often miss. But memories change, so a historian checks the details against records and other accounts, weighing the memory as they would any source.

steps.cue: Keep your attention on the speaker through a long answer, noting follow-ups quietly.
steps.holdBreakNote: Your attention wandered. Bring it back to the speaker.
steps.prompt: Keep your attention on the speaker through a long answer, noting follow-ups quietly.
steps.title: Keep listening through a long answer
steps.why: Long answers are where the richest stories are, and staying attentive through them shows respect as well as catching details worth asking about. Noting follow-ups quietly lets you return to them without interrupting the flow.

steps.cue: Write who was interviewed, when, what they agreed to and a summary.
steps.prompt: Write who was interviewed, when, what they agreed to and a summary.
steps.title: Record the archive notes
steps.why: An archive note tells future listeners what the recording is and what they may do with it. Writing the consent terms beside the summary protects the interviewee and makes the recording useful for years.

steps.cue: Thank them and confirm what they are happy for the class archive to keep.
steps.prompt: Thank them and confirm what they are happy for the class archive to keep.
steps.title: Thank the interviewee and check the sharing
steps.why: Closing with thanks and a check of what may be kept respects the gift of their story. It gives them the last word on how it is used, which is at the heart of every ethical oral history project.

steps.cue: What did the interview teach you that a book could not? What was hard?
steps.prompt: What did the interview teach you that a book could not? What was hard?
steps.title: Check in at the end of the session
steps.why: Interviewers debrief after every recording, so the class does too: each learner says what their question drew out and what they would ask differently. Speaking about consent and listening in front of the group is practice for the real interviews, and it shows the archivist who is ready to lead one.

supportLine: your teacher, a school counsellor or a trusted adult at home — if anything in this lesson was hard, talk it through afterwards
tagline: Ask consent, ask open questions, then listen — a memory is a source, not a verdict
